name: Name
description: The website's address, with `www.` removed if it starts with that
description - details: This creates one consistent way to refer to a website, regardless of whether `www.` happens to be present or absent. This is the field most useful for counting how many distinct websites appear in the data (though see the caveat on `redirect` and `url` about why one website can still appear as more than one row).

name: Initial URL
description: The web address that the scanner started with, before anything happened
description - details: This is simply `https://` plus the address from the website list (the `initial_domain` field). It is the starting point, not necessarily where the scan ended up. See `url` for where it actually landed. Example: `https://science.nasa.gov`.
queryable: Yes, exact match, by looking the address up directly: /v1/websites/{address} (use the address alone, without `https://` — for example /v1/websites/10x.gsa.gov)

name: Initial Domain
description: The address that the scanner started with, without the `https://` in front of it
description - details: In technical terms this is a Fully Qualified Domain Name — the full address of one specific website, such as `science.nasa.gov`, as opposed to the broader `nasa.gov`. It never includes a path (nothing after a `/`). Example: `science.nasa.gov` or `t.mil`.

name: Initial Base Domain
description: The agency-level portion of the starting address — the part that was actually registered
description - details: An address like `science.nasa.gov` is a more specific location within the broader, registered name `nasa.gov`. This field strips away everything in front of that registered name, so that every website belonging to one agency's domain can be grouped together. Example: `nasa.gov` or `p.mil`.

name: Initial Top Level Domain
description: The last segment of the starting address, such as `.gov` or `.mil`
description - details: Nearly every address in this data ends in `gov` or `mil`, with a small number ending in `com` or `edu` for sites run by agencies on those domains. Written here without the leading period, e.g. `gov` rather than `.gov`.

name: Redirect
description: Whether the website sent the scanner somewhere other than where it started
description - details: A great many government web addresses automatically forward visitors to a different address — most often adding `www.` or switching from `http` to `https`. This field compares where the scan started (`initial_domain`) to where it landed (`name`) and says whether they differ. Because of this, the same website can appear more than once in this data under different starting addresses that all forward to it — so counting rows is not the same as counting websites.

name: URL
description: The web address the scanner ended up looking at, after any redirects finished
description - details: If the starting address (`initial_url`) didn't forward anywhere else, this will be the same address. If it did forward somewhere else, this is the final destination — the page that was actually scanned and that every other field in this row describes.

name: Domain
description: The final address, without the `https://` in front of it
description - details: Same idea as `initial_domain`, but for where the scan ended up rather than where it started. In technical terms this is a Fully Qualified Domain Name — a full, specific address such as `www.science.nasa.gov`. Blank whenever the scan never successfully loaded a page.

name: Base Domain
description: The agency-level portion of the final address — the part that was actually registered
description - details: Same idea as `initial_base_domain`, but based on where the scan ended up. Use this field to group every website that ultimately belongs to one agency's registered domain, even if some of them got there by redirecting from somewhere else.

name: Top Level Domain
description: The last segment of the final address, such as `.gov` or `.mil`
description - details: Same idea as `initial_top_level_domain`, but based on where the scan ended up. Written without the leading period.

name: Live
description: Whether the website responded the way a normal, working page should
description - details: Specifically, this is `TRUE` only if the server's reply code was 200, 201, 202, 203, 204, 205, or 206 — the family of codes that mean 'here's your page.' Anything else (an error, a login wall, a dead domain) is `FALSE`. Blank only if the scan never got a reply at all.

name: Filter
description: Whether this address is suspected of not really being a public website
description - details: Two separate processes can mark an address this way: (1) before scanning, if the address matches a known pattern for things like staging sites or admin login pages, and (2) after scanning, if the page that came back turned out to be a data file (like XML or JSON) meant for other computers rather than a page for people to read. `TRUE` means the address is excluded from the 'live, filtered' download that most people should start with.

name: Status Code
description: The three-digit code the website's server sent back
description - details: This is the standard web code a server uses to describe what happened. Codes starting with 2 mean success; codes starting with 4 mean the visitor did something the server didn't like (like asking for a page that doesn't exist); codes starting with 5 mean the server itself had a problem. Codes starting with 3 mean the server redirected elsewhere — in practice this does occasionally show up here, when the final hop in a redirect chain happens to also redirect.

name: Media Type
description: What kind of file the server said it was sending back
description - details: Most pages meant for people to read report `text/html`. Anything else — such as `application/json` or `application/xml` — usually means the address serves data for other computers to consume rather than a page for a person to view, and may be excluded by the `filter` field as a result. Shows `none-specified` when the server didn't say what kind of file it was sending.

name: Agency
description: The federal agency that owns this website's registered address
description - details: For `.gov` addresses, this is the organization that officially registered the domain. For addresses on other endings (like `.mil`, `.com`, or `.edu`), it's our best estimate of which agency runs it. Blank on a small number of rows (well under 1%) where ownership could not be determined.
queryable: Yes, exact match — parameter `target_url_agency_owner` (example: target_url_agency_owner=General Services Administration)

name: Bureau
description: The specific office or sub-organization within the agency that owns this website
description - details: A more specific breakdown than `agency` — for example, within the Department of Health and Human Services, this field might say 'National Institutes of Health.' Blank on roughly 1 in 5 rows, where the registering organization didn't break down to this level of detail.
queryable: Yes, exact match — parameter `target_url_bureau_owner` (example: target_url_bureau_owner=National Institutes of Health)

name: Branch
description: Which branch of the federal government owns this website
description - details: One of Executive, Legislative, Judicial, or (on a handful of rows) Federal, for cases that don't neatly fit the other three. The large majority of rows are Executive branch.
queryable: Not currently filterable through the API, even though it may appear so — a `branch` parameter is accepted but silently ignored, and all results are returned regardless of its value.

name: 404 Test
description: Whether the website correctly tells visitors when a page doesn't exist
description - details: A well-built website should respond to a request for a nonexistent page by saying so clearly (a '404 Not Found' reply) rather than quietly showing a normal-looking page. This is tested by taking the starting address and tacking on a random, made-up page name, then checking what comes back. `TRUE` means the site behaved correctly; `FALSE` means it either showed a normal page anyway or the check itself failed to get a clear answer (for example, because the site was unreachable) — so `FALSE` does not always mean the site is misconfigured.

name: Data Source
description: Which of the lists used to build the master website directory included this address
description - details: The complete directory of federal websites that gets scanned every day is built by combining dozens of separate public lists (one from the Digital Analytics Program, one from the official .gov registry, one from past Congressional directories, and so on) and removing duplicates. This field names every list this particular address appeared on. An address can be on several lists at once.

name: Scan Status - Date
description: When this row's data was last written to the database
description - details: In most cases, this is within seconds of when the scan actually ran. However, a separate weekly process updates two other fields (`pageviews`/`visits` and the HTTPS/HSTS security fields) for every row at once, and that process currently also resets this date — even for rows that were not otherwise rescanned. In practice this means a recent date here does not always guarantee the rest of the row's data is fresh; check the individual `*_scan_status` fields for that.

name: Scan Status - Secondary Data Dates
description: When the outside data sources used for traffic and security information were last updated
description - details: The `pageviews` and `visits` fields come from a file maintained by analytics.usa.gov; the `https_enforced` and `hsts` fields come from a file maintained by CISA. Rather than dates for this row specifically, these are the dates those two outside files themselves were last refreshed — the same two dates appear on every row. Shown as text in the form {"dap":"YYYY-MM-DD","https":"YYYY-MM-DD"}.

name: Scan Status - Primary
description: Whether the main check of this website finished successfully
description - details: `completed` means it worked. Anything else is an error code explaining what went wrong (for example, the site took too long to respond, or its address couldn't be found at all) — the full list of codes and what each one means is explained at https://github.com/GSA/site-scanning-documentation/blob/main/pages/scan_statuses.md. When this is anything other than `completed`, most of the other fields in this row will be blank, because the scanner never got far enough to collect them.
queryable: Not currently filterable through the API — a `scan_status` parameter is accepted but currently causes the request to fail with a server error.

name: Scan Status - Accessibility
description: Whether the check for accessibility problems finished successfully
description - details: `completed` means it worked and `accessibility_violations` reflects the result. Anything else is an error code, explained at https://github.com/GSA/site-scanning-documentation/blob/main/pages/scan_statuses.md.

name: Scan Status - DNS
description: Whether the check of this website's network records finished successfully
description - details: `completed` means it worked. Anything else is an error code, explained at https://github.com/GSA/site-scanning-documentation/blob/main/pages/scan_statuses.md.

name: Scan Status - Not Found
description: Whether the "page not found" check finished successfully
description - details: `completed` means it worked and `404_test` reflects the result. Anything else is an error code, explained at https://github.com/GSA/site-scanning-documentation/blob/main/pages/scan_statuses.md.

name: Scan Status - Performance
description: Whether the page-speed check finished successfully
description - details: `completed` means it worked and `cumulative_layout_shift`/`largest_contentful_paint` reflect the result. Anything else is an error code, explained at https://github.com/GSA/site-scanning-documentation/blob/main/pages/scan_statuses.md.

name: Scan Status - Robots.txt
description: Whether the check of the site's robots.txt file finished successfully
description - details: `completed` means it worked. Anything else is an error code, explained at https://github.com/GSA/site-scanning-documentation/blob/main/pages/scan_statuses.md.

name: Scan Status - Security
description: Whether the HTTPS/security lookup finished successfully
description - details: Unlike the other scans, this one doesn't load the website directly — it looks up the address in a separate security dataset maintained by CISA. `completed` means a matching entry was found. Roughly 1 in 4 rows show an error here simply because the address wasn't present in that outside dataset, not because of a problem with the website itself.

name: Scan Status - Sitemap.xml
description: Whether the check of the site's sitemap.xml file finished successfully
description - details: `completed` means it worked. Anything else is an error code, explained at https://github.com/GSA/site-scanning-documentation/blob/main/pages/scan_statuses.md.

name: Scan Status - WWW
description: Whether the check of the "www." version of this address finished successfully
description - details: This check takes the starting address and adds `www.` to the front, then tries to load it, to see whether the site requires or forbids that prefix. On about 4 out of 5 rows this shows `dns_resolution_error` — not because of a problem with the site, but because the starting address already pointed at a specific sub-location (like `science.nasa.gov`), and adding `www.` in front of that produces an address that was never meant to exist (`www.science.nasa.gov`). This is expected and not a sign of a broken website.

name: Homepage Fingerprint
description: A short code that summarizes everything on the page, used to detect whether a page has changed
description - details: This is not a meaningful code to read on its own — it's created by running the page's full content through a standard scrambling formula (called MD5) that turns any amount of text into one fixed-length code. Its only use is comparison: if this code is identical between two scans of the same address, the page is almost certainly unchanged; if it's different, the page may have changed, or it may just contain something that changes on its own (like a timestamp or a rotating news item) even though nobody edited it. For that reason, an unchanged code is strong evidence a page is untouched, but a changed code is weak evidence anything meaningful happened. This measures the page as the browser rendered it, after any on-page scripts ran — not the raw file the server originally sent.

name: Accessibility - Violations
description: A count of accessibility problems found on the page, grouped by category
description - details: Shown as text listing each category and how many instances of it were found, for example {"contrast":2,"language":1} — meaning 2 color-contrast problems and 1 language-related problem. This is detected with axe-core, a popular accessibility scanning tool commonly used by accessibility professionals. This only catches problems a computer can detect automatically; it is not a substitute for a human accessibility review, and a blank result does not guarantee a page is fully accessible — it may also mean the check could not finish (see `accessibility_scan_status`).

name: Analytics - Pageviews
description: How many times pages on this website were viewed over the last 30 days
description - details: Sourced from the Digital Analytics Program's public traffic report at analytics.usa.gov, which only covers sites that have that tracking code installed. Blank, not zero, when a site isn't in that report.

name: Analytics - Visits
description: How many separate visits this website received over the last 30 days
description - details: A "visit" counts one person's full session on the site, as opposed to `pageviews`, which counts every individual page they looked at during that session. Sourced from the same Digital Analytics Program report as `pageviews`, and blank for the same reason.

name: DNS - IPv6
description: Whether this website's network setup supports the newer IPv6 internet addressing standard
description - details: Nearly every website still works over the older IPv4 standard; this field indicates whether it also supports IPv6, which is a modernization goal for federal systems. `TRUE` means a matching network record (called an AAAA record) was found.

name: DNS - Hostname
description: The name of the hosting or cloud service this website appears to run on, if recognizable
description - details: This looks at the website's underlying network address and checks whether it matches one of a short list of well-known cloud and content-delivery providers (such as Amazon's `amazonaws.com` or Cloudflare's `cloudflare.com`). Blank doesn't mean the site has no host — it means the host wasn't one on that short recognized list.

name: Infrastructure - CMS Provider
description: The content management system (the software) a website appears to be built on, if recognizable
description - details: Checks the page's code against the signatures of 63 different publicly known content management systems — the most common ones actually found on federal sites are Drupal, WordPress, and cloud.gov Pages. Blank means no recognizable match was found, not that the site has no underlying software.

name: Infrastructure - Login Provider
description: The outside identity service a site appears to use for signing in, if recognizable
description - details: Checks sign-in links on the page against a short list of well-known providers, such as login.gov or Okta. Blank means either the site doesn't have a detectable sign-in link, or it uses a provider not on that list.

name: Infrastructure - Login Detected
description: Signs that the page has a sign-in form, listed as the specific clues that were found
description - details: Rather than a simple yes/no, this lists which specific telltale signs were spotted in the page's code — for example a password field, or text reading "Sign In." Shown as a list of the matching clues. Blank means none of the known clues were found, which usually (but not always) means there's no login form.

name: Infrastructure - Site Search Detected
description: Whether the page appears to have a search box
description - details: Looks for the common code patterns a search box leaves behind — a form intended for search, or an input field clearly meant for typing a search term.

name: Infrastructure - Search.gov Detected
description: Whether the page specifically uses the government's shared Search.gov tool
description - details: Search.gov is a search service that many federal sites use instead of building their own. This field looks for the specific code pattern that tool leaves behind. Unlike most yes/no fields in this data, this one is never explicitly `FALSE` — it is either `TRUE` or blank, because the check only confirms a detection and doesn't rule one out.

name: Infrastructure - DAP Detected
description: Whether the page uses the government's shared web-traffic tracking tool, the Digital Analytics Program (DAP)
description - details: DAP is an analytics snippet used to measure traffic government-wide; it's what generates the `pageviews` and `visits` figures seen elsewhere in this data (via a separate outside report). This field looks for that snippet directly in the page's code.

name: Infrastructure - DAP Parameters
description: The specific agency/sub-agency codes the site has configured inside its DAP tracking snippet
description - details: Agencies can customize the DAP snippet with their own identifying codes, for example {"agency":"NASA","subagency":"GSFC"}. Blank whenever `dap` is `FALSE`, or when DAP is present but hosted in a way that hides these details from the scanner.

name: Infrastructure - DAP Version
description: Which version of the DAP tracking snippet the site is running
description - details: Useful mainly for spotting sites running an outdated version of the shared analytics snippet. Example: `20260107 v8.8 - GA4`.

name: Infrastructure - Google Analytics Tag ID
description: Any Google Analytics tracking codes found on the page, besides the shared DAP one
description - details: Some sites run their own separate Google Analytics tracking in addition to (or instead of) the government-wide DAP tool. When more than one is found, they're listed together separated by commas.

name: Infrastructure - Third Party Service Domains
description: The outside companies' addresses that this page loads content from
description - details: When a page loads, it often pulls in images, scripts, fonts, or trackers from other companies' servers — this is a list of the distinct outside addresses involved, such as `fonts.googleapis.com` or `www.googletagmanager.com`. Useful for seeing how much a site depends on outside services, and for privacy/security review.

name: Infrastructure - Third Party Service URLs
description: The exact outside web addresses this page loads content from
description - details: A more detailed version of `third_party_service_domains` — rather than just the company name, this lists the full specific address of each outside file that was loaded.

name: Infrastructure - Third Party Service Count
description: How many distinct outside companies' addresses this page loads content from
description - details: A simple count of the items in `third_party_service_domains`. Shows `0`, not blank, when a page loads nothing from the outside.

name: Infrastructure - Cookie Domains
description: The addresses that set a tracking or session cookie when this page loaded
description - details: A cookie is a small piece of data a website asks your browser to remember. This lists every distinct address that asked to set one while this page loaded, which can include the site itself as well as outside tracking services.

name: Infrastructure - Hyperlink Domains
description: Every distinct address that this page links out to
description - details: A list of every website address found inside the page's clickable links, both to other pages on the same site and to entirely different websites.

name: Infrastructure - Tooling
description: Front-end design tools and code libraries detected on the page
description - details: Checks the page's code for the signatures of 44 widely used front-end tools, grouped into four kinds: visual design frameworks (like Bootstrap or Tailwind), app-building frameworks (like React or Angular), general-purpose code libraries (like jQuery), and pre-built visual component sets (like Material UI).

name: Mobile - Viewport Meta Tag Detected
description: Whether the page is correctly set up to resize for phone screens
description - details: Checks for a specific line of code in the page (a `viewport` meta tag) that tells phone browsers how to scale the page. This is one of the most basic requirements for a mobile-friendly website; its absence usually means the site will look poorly sized on a phone.

name: Performance - Cumulative Layout Shift
description: A score for how much the page's layout visibly jumps around while it loads
description - details: Measured as a plain number with no unit, where `0` means the page didn't shift at all after it started rendering, and higher numbers mean more unexpected movement — things jumping around on screen as a visitor is trying to read or click. This is one of the standard web-performance measurements used industry-wide (one of Google's "Core Web Vitals").

name: Performance - Largest Contentful Paint
description: How long it took, in milliseconds, for the main visible content of the page to finish loading
description - details: Measured from when the page started loading to when what's likely the largest, most prominent piece of content (often a headline or hero image) finished appearing on screen. Lower is faster. 1,000 milliseconds equals one second. This is one of the standard web-performance measurements used industry-wide (one of Google's "Core Web Vitals").

name: Required Links - URL
description: Which commonly-required federal website links were found, based on the links' web addresses
description - details: Federal websites are expected to link to certain standard pages — things like an About page, a Privacy policy, a FOIA (public records request) page, or an Inspector General hotline, per digital.gov/resources/required-web-content-and-links — plus a Spanish-language version of the site, if one exists. This field lists which of those were found by checking whether a short recognizable snippet appears anywhere in a link's web address (not the visible text of the link — see `required_links_text` for that). A link only needs to contain the snippet, not match it exactly.

name: Required Links - Text
description: Which commonly-required federal website links were found, based on the links' visible text
description - details: The same list of commonly-required pages as `required_links_url`, but checked a different way — by looking for a short recognizable snippet anywhere inside a link's visible, clickable text (for example, a link whose text reads "View our Privacy Policy" would match on "privacy policy"). A link only needs to contain the snippet, not match it exactly.

name: Required Links - Feedback
description: Which feedback-related links were found on the page, based on the links' visible text
description - details: Looks for links whose visible, clickable text reads as one specific feedback-related word or phrase, such as "feedback," "contact," or "help." Unlike `required_links_text`, this field requires the link's visible text to match one of those words exactly — a link reading "Contact Us" or "Contact us" would not count, because neither is an exact match for "contact."

name: Security - HTTPS Required
description: Whether the website forces visitors into a secure (HTTPS) connection
description - details: A properly secured site should refuse to let a visitor stay on the insecure `http://` version and should automatically send them to the secure `https://` version instead. This comes from a separate dataset maintained by CISA (the government's cybersecurity agency), not from our own scan of the page — see `security_scan_status`.

name: Security - HSTS Preloaded
description: Whether browsers are instructed to always connect to this site securely, even before the first visit
description - details: HSTS ("HTTP Strict Transport Security") is a stronger version of the HTTPS protection above: once a site is set up this way, a browser will refuse to connect to it insecurely at all — including on someone's very first visit, before the site has had a chance to say anything. `TRUE` if the site is on the official preload list, or if it otherwise strongly enforces this setting. Comes from the same CISA-maintained dataset as `https_enforced`.

name: SEO - title
description: The page's title, as it appears in a browser tab or search result
description - details: This is the text set by the page's `<title>` tag — the single most basic piece of information search engines and browser tabs use to identify a page. Shown as an empty value, not blank, on some rows where the site set a title tag but left it empty.

name: SEO - description
description: The short summary of the page that the site provided for search engines
description - details: This is the text set by the page's description meta tag — the summary a search engine often displays underneath a page's title in search results. Written by the site's authors, not auto-generated by anything in this program.

name: SEO - keywords
description: A list of topic words the site's authors tagged the page with for search engines
description - details: An older search-engine optimization practice, now largely ignored by major search engines, where a site lists topic words directly in its code. Still present on some sites and can hint at how actively a site's technical setup is maintained.

name: Open Graph - og:title
description: The page's title, specifically as it should appear when shared on social media
description - details: "Open Graph" is a standard that lets a site control how it looks when a link to it is shared on social media or in a chat app — this is the title portion of that. Often the same as the `title` field, but can be written separately.

name: Open Graph - og:description
description: The page's description, specifically as it should appear when shared on social media
description - details: The social-media-preview counterpart to `description`, using the same Open Graph standard.

name: Open Graph - article:published_time
description: When the page's content was first published, if the site provided that date
description - details: Only present on sites that mark their content as a dated article (such as a news release or blog post) using the Open Graph standard. Most pages, including most homepages, don't set this.

name: Open Graph - article:modified_time
description: When the page's content was last updated, if the site provided that date
description - details: The update-date counterpart to `og_article_published`, using the same Open Graph standard.

name: Open Graph - og:image
description: The image the site wants shown when this page is shared on social media
description - details: The social-media-preview image, as specified by the site using the Open Graph standard.

name: Open Graph - og:type
description: What kind of content the site says this page is, using the Open Graph standard
description - details: Common values are `website` for a general page or `article` for a dated piece of content like a news release.

name: Open Graph - og:url
description: The address the site says this page's social-media preview should link to
description - details: Normally the same as the page's actual address, but a site can set this to point somewhere else using the Open Graph standard.

name: Other Tags - Canonical Link
description: The address the site says is the "real" or preferred version of this page
description - details: Sites sometimes have the same content reachable at more than one address (for example, with or without a trailing slash). A canonical link is the site's own way of telling search engines which address is the one to treat as authoritative.

name: Other Tags - Language
description: The main language the page says it's written in
description - details: Comes from a specific code in the page (the `lang` attribute) — for example `en` for English or `es` for Spanish. This should be set on every properly built page; its absence is itself a basic accessibility and search-engine problem.

name: Other Tags - Language Links
description: Which other languages the site offers this same page in, if it says so
description - details: Some multilingual sites include a tag listing the other language versions of the current page are available in — for example a page might list `en,es` to indicate it also exists in Spanish.

name: Other Tags - Main Element Detected
description: Whether the page's code marks which part of it is the main content
description - details: Checks for a `<main>` tag — a standard way of telling browsers and screen readers which part of the page is the primary content, as opposed to navigation menus, headers, and footers. Its presence is considered good accessibility practice.

name: Robots.txt - Detected
description: Whether the site has a working robots.txt file in the correct location
description - details: A robots.txt file tells automated crawlers (like search engines) which parts of a site they're allowed to visit. This field is `TRUE` only if the file loads successfully (see `robots_txt_status_code`) and lives at exactly the expected location — the top level of the site, immediately after the domain name. A robots.txt file that exists but only works from a different folder does not count, since the standard requires it to live at the top level.

name: Robots.txt - Final URL
description: The exact address the robots.txt file was found at, after any redirects
description - details: Normally just the site's address with `/robots.txt` added, but if that address redirected elsewhere, this shows where it ended up.

name: Robots.txt - Final URL - Status Code
description: The three-digit reply code the server sent back when asked for the robots.txt file
description - details: Same meaning as the main `status_code` field, but specifically for the robots.txt file rather than the site's homepage. A `404` here means the site simply doesn't have one.

name: Robots.txt - Final URL - Media Type
description: What kind of file the server said the robots.txt address was
description - details: A correctly set up robots.txt file is typically `text/plain`, though some misconfigured sites return `text/html` here instead (often because the address serves an error page rather than an actual robots.txt file).

name: Robots.txt - Final URL - Filesize
description: The size of the robots.txt file, in bytes
description - details: One byte is roughly one typed character. A typical robots.txt file is a few hundred to a few thousand bytes. Blank when the file wasn't found.

name: Robots.txt - Crawl Delay
description: How many seconds the site's robots.txt file asks automated crawlers to wait between requests
description - details: Not every site sets this; it's an optional instruction some sites use to reduce server load from search-engine crawlers and similar automated visitors. Blank when the file doesn't specify one — this is normal and does not indicate a problem.

name: Robots.txt - Sitemap Locations
description: Any sitemap addresses the site's robots.txt file points to
description - details: A site's robots.txt file can list the address of its sitemap.xml file (see the Sitemap.xml fields below) so crawlers can find it easily. This can be a different address than the one this program checks directly in the `sitemap_xml_*` fields. Like most list-type fields in the downloadable spreadsheet version of this data, this is cut off at 2,000 characters if it runs long; the JSON version of this data is not cut off.

name: Sitemap.xml - Detected
description: Whether the site has a working sitemap.xml file
description - details: A sitemap.xml file is a list of a site's pages meant to help search engines find everything on it. This field is `TRUE` if an address was found that both responds successfully and is recognizable as a sitemap — either because its address matches one of the standard naming patterns (such as ending in `/sitemap.xml`), or because the file it returned was itself identified as an XML file.

name: Sitemap.xml - Final URL
description: The exact address the sitemap.xml file was found at, after any redirects
description - details: Normally just the site's address with `/sitemap.xml` added, but if that address redirected elsewhere, this shows where it ended up.

name: Sitemap.xml - Final URL - Status Code
description: The three-digit reply code the server sent back when asked for the sitemap.xml file
description - details: Same meaning as the main `status_code` field, but specifically for the sitemap.xml file. A `404` here means the site simply doesn't have one at the standard address.

name: Sitemap.xml - Final URL - Media Type
description: What kind of file the server said the sitemap.xml address was
description - details: A correctly set up sitemap is typically `application/xml` or `text/xml`. Some sites instead return `text/html` here, often because the address serves an error page rather than an actual sitemap.

name: Sitemap.xml - Final URL - Filesize
description: The size of the sitemap.xml file, in bytes
description - details: One byte is roughly one typed character. Larger sites tend to have much larger sitemap files, since each listed page adds to the size. Blank when no sitemap was found.

name: Sitemap.xml - Items Count
description: How many individual page addresses are listed directly inside the sitemap.xml file
description - details: Important caveat: large websites often don't list every page in one file. Instead, their main sitemap.xml is just a table of contents pointing to several smaller sitemap files. When that's the case, this field counts `0` — not because the site has no pages listed anywhere, but because none of the page listings are in this particular file. In today's data, well over half of the rows with a value here show exactly `0`, and many of those are large, well-maintained sites. A `0` should not be read as "this site has no sitemap."

name: Sitemap.xml - Last Modified
description: The most recent "last updated" date listed inside the sitemap.xml file
description - details: Sitemaps can optionally tag each listed page with the date it was last updated; this field reports the single most recent of those dates. Blank if the sitemap doesn't include any such dates.

name: Sitemap.xml - PDF Count
description: A rough count of how many times "`.pdf`" appears in the sitemap.xml file
description - details: This counts occurrences of the text `.pdf` anywhere in the sitemap file's contents, as a rough stand-in for how many PDF documents the site lists. Because it's a plain text search rather than a count of actual PDF links, it can occasionally overcount or undercount in unusual cases.

name: Sitemap.xml - Fingerprint
description: A short code that summarizes the sitemap.xml page's contents, used to detect whether it has changed
description - details: Works the same way as `page_hash`, but for the sitemap.xml address instead of the homepage — see that field's explanation for how to interpret it, including the caveat that an unchanged code is stronger evidence than a changed one.

name: USWDS - Favicon
description: Whether the standard U.S. Web Design System icon file is referenced in the page's code
description - details: USWDS (the U.S. Web Design System) is the government's shared visual design toolkit, used to give federal sites a consistent, recognizable look. This specific field checks for the small icon file that's part of USWDS's standard header. Shown as a point value (`0` or `20`) that feeds into the overall `uswds_count` score below, rather than a plain yes/no.

name: USWDS - Favicon in CSS
description: Whether the standard U.S. Web Design System icon file is referenced in the page's style sheet
description - details: The same check as `uswds_favicon`, but looking in the page's CSS (its separate styling file) rather than its main code.

name: USWDS - Public Sans Font
description: Whether the page's style sheet references "Public Sans," the standard USWDS font
description - details: Public Sans is a web font that ships with USWDS; this checks whether the page's styling references it.

name: USWDS - In-page CSS
description: How many times a USWDS-style class name shows up in styling written directly inside the page
description - details: USWDS components are typically named starting with `usa-` (for example `usa-banner`). This counts how many times that pattern appears inside a `<style>` block written directly in the page's own code, as opposed to in a separate style sheet file.

name: USWDS - USA Class List
description: Which specific USWDS component names were found used on the page
description - details: A list of the distinct `usa-`-prefixed component names detected (for example `usa-banner`, `usa-footer`), with any more specific sub-variants trimmed off so that related components are grouped together.

name: USWDS - Here's How Link
description: Whether the standard "official website of the United States government" banner is present
description - details: This is the familiar banner near the top of most federal sites that reads "Here's how you know" (or, on Spanish-language pages, its Spanish equivalent) and explains how to verify a site is official. It's one of the most visible and recognizable parts of USWDS.

name: USWDS - USA Classes
description: A score based on how many different USWDS component names are used on the page
description - details: Rather than a plain count, this is a formula-based score: more distinct `usa-`-prefixed components in use produces a higher number, but the scale isn't 1-to-1 with the raw count. Feeds into the overall `uswds_count` score below.

name: USWDS - USA Elements List
description: Which specific USWDS custom HTML tags were found used on the page
description - details: USWDS most often works through ordinary HTML with special class names (see `uswds_usa_class_list`), but it also offers a small number of genuinely custom HTML tags. This field currently only checks for one such tag, `usa-banner`, so it is populated far less often than the other USWDS fields — a blank result here does not mean a site isn't using USWDS.

name: USWDS - String
description: How many times the literal word "uswds" appears anywhere in the page's code
description - details: A simple text search used as one more signal that a site is built with the U.S. Web Design System, often because the toolkit's own files mention its name directly.

name: USWDS - String in CSS
description: Whether the literal word "uswds" appears anywhere in the page's style sheet
description - details: The same idea as `uswds_string`, but checking the page's separate CSS styling file rather than its main code.

name: USWDS - Semantic Version
description: Which specific release of the U.S. Web Design System the site appears to be running, if it can be determined
description - details: USWDS, like most software, has numbered releases (for example `v2.13.3` or `v3.12.0`). This is detected from a version number mentioned directly in the site's style sheet, so it's only available when a site's styling happens to include that detail — many sites using USWDS will still show blank here.

name: USWDS - Version
description: A point value credited toward the overall USWDS score if any specific version number was detected
description - details: This is not itself a version number — it's simply `100` if `uswds_semantic_version` found something and `0` if it didn't. It exists as one more ingredient feeding into the overall `uswds_count` score below.

name: USWDS - Count
description: An overall score estimating how fully the page uses the U.S. Web Design System
description - details: This is not a count of anything in particular — it's a single combined score built by adding together several of the other USWDS fields above (favicon, font, classes, version, and so on), each worth different amounts. A higher number suggests heavier USWDS use; `0` suggests none was detected. It does not include two of the other USWDS fields above, `uswds_usa_elements_list` and `uswds_banner_heres_how`, in its formula.

name: WWW - URL
description: The address that resulted from adding "www." to the front of the starting address and loading it
description - details: This exists to check whether a site requires or forbids the `www.` prefix. Blank on roughly 4 out of 5 rows — see the note on `www_scan_status` for why that's expected rather than a sign of a problem.

name: WWW - Status Code
description: The three-digit reply code the server sent back for the "www."-prefixed address
description - details: Same meaning as the main `status_code` field, but for the version of the address with `www.` added to the front.

name: WWW - Title
description: The page title found at the "www."-prefixed address
description - details: Same meaning as the main `title` field, but for the version of the address with `www.` added to the front.

name: WWW - Same
description: Whether the "www."-prefixed address led to the exact same final address as the original
description - details: `TRUE` means adding `www.` to the front made no real difference — both versions end up at the identical destination. This field is currently only available through the API, not in the downloadable spreadsheet or JSON snapshot files.
